analysis.title: GREED & fear: The case for a peak in AI capex
key_insights: Christopher Wood argues the AI capex cycle may have peaked or entered a mid-cycle correction, even though real-world capex data does not yet show it. Markets are signalling a growing unwillingness to fund AI investment.

Mid-term results were an expected Republican rout. Brent fell 8.7% on 4 Nov on hopes Trump abandons the Iran project, which Wood rates a 50/50 possibility. Bonds rallied on hopes of Democratic restraint on spending. Semiconductors sold off again on worries that Democrats will focus on data centers and AI regulation.

AI capex contributed 1.39ppts, or 67%, of US real GDP growth of 2.1% YoY in the four quarters to 3Q26. Nominal investment in information processing equipment and software reached a record 5.35% of GDP in 3Q26, up from 5.05% in 2Q26 and above the 4.46% peak in 4Q00.

Credit is the key signal. Amazon, Alphabet and Meta 10-year spreads over Treasuries rose from lows of 73bp, 65bp and 94bp on 12 October to 89bp, 81bp and 129bp. Oracle 5Y CDS rose from 153bp in early June to 329bp on 20 October, and CoreWeave from 452bp to 1,163bp on 22 October. SoftBank 5Y CDS rose from 278bp to 442bp.
The base case is that AI credit stress will end the capex arms race: the credit card gets taken away. Consensus 2027 capex for the four major hyperscalers is US$1.04tn, which Wood thinks is too high.

CoreWeave contracts of 3-7 years are priced at about US$12-15m/MW annualised, versus about US$40m/MW for 3-6 month deals, roughly three times higher. This suggests little desire to lock in rental prices beyond one year and little confidence that chip demand persists. CoreWeave raised prices about 25% in July.

CoreWeave's US$3.1bn DDTL 5.0 GPU-backed facility has fallen 2% in price since mid-June. Its yield to maturity rose 74bp from 7.62% to 8.36%. Data center securitization issuance rose to US$27bn in 2025 and is projected at US$40bn this year. Financing is largely off balance sheet through special purpose vehicles with private credit.

Jefferies quant strategist Desh Peramunetilleke argues for diversifying beyond AI. Global AI stocks' consensus earnings growth is expected to slow from about 100% in 2026 to 30% in 2027 and 22% in 2028.

In 3Q26 the four hyperscalers' combined capex rose 108% YoY to US$202bn. Microsoft cut 2026 capex guidance from US$175bn to US$170bn on delayed third-party capacity but expects acceleration in 1H27. Amazon held US$220bn, Alphabet held US$195-205bn, and Meta raised to US$135-145bn from US$130-145bn.

The market focused on AI cannibalising legacy businesses. Google search revenue grew 12% YoY to US$63bn (19% in 1Q26, 17% in 2Q26) while Google Cloud grew 103% to US$30.7bn. Search fell below half of Alphabet revenue at 49.7%. Amazon online stores grew 2% YoY to US$68.5bn (15% in 2Q26) while AWS grew 39% to US$46bn.
Amazon and Alphabet free cash flow was negative US$35bn and US$9bn in 3Q26, yet both plan to keep spending. Microsoft free cash flow was still positive at US$18.6bn.

Hyperscalers are in a prisoner's dilemma: damned if they spend, damned if they don't. Tax deductibility under the OBBBA (100% bonus depreciation made permanent) is a further spending motive. Democrats including Senator Warren want to repeal it and sent letters to Meta, Alphabet, Amazon and Microsoft in late September.

Wood's base case is that the end game is massive capital destruction as hyperscalers fail to earn adequate returns, because AI lacks Internet-style winner-takes-all network effects. Circular financing is the key US vulnerability. RPOs of Microsoft, Amazon, Alphabet and Oracle reached US$2.5tn last quarter, which only works if parts of the AI ecosystem are seen as too big to fail.

Microsoft is offering voluntary exit buyouts to about 60,000 eligible employees, more than a quarter of its workforce. Wood calls it the best example so far of AI-linked white-collar job losses. A Democratic administration may be less willing to treat AI as too big to fail, especially if AI hits employment.

China AI semiconductor Top 10 Index rose 109% in USD in 1H26 to a late-June peak, then fell 50% since, versus a 1% decline in MSCI China over the same period. Z.ai is down 84% from its HK$2,980 intraday peak in late June.

China AI labs focus on compute efficiency and commercial applications rather than AGI. Capex is about 100% of cloud revenue for Alibaba and Tencent versus about 130% for US hyperscalers. Wood expects the US to move toward cost focus. Chinese inference demand is strong and compute is the constraint: an H100 8-GPU server rents for about Rmb100,000/month.

Elon Musk predicted 'guppy-level death and consolidation' among more than 200 neoclouds without substantial revenue independent of AI data centers. A reported AI math result turned out to be regurgitated unpublished research, prompting corporates such as law firms to run open-weight Chinese models like Kimi and DeepSeek on premises.

A mid-cycle correction has already happened in market terms: memory stocks are down 40% from their late-June peak. A speaker close to TSMC said it remains on course to spend US$75-80bn next year and US$100bn in 2028.
A credit-triggered AI capex slowdown would hit US growth and reverse Fed expectations from tightening to easing. Gold traded near the bottom of Wood's US$3,800-4,000/oz consolidation range.

Treasuries will not provide the usual flight-to-quality in an AI capex bust because of fiscal dominance. The deficit is 6.2% of GDP, and it normally rises about 6 points of GDP in a recession. The 10-year yield is down 49bp from the 5.36% peak on 7 October. Wood would sell bonds into that rally.

US biotech is recovering, with the SPDR S&P Biotech ETF up 139% from its April 2025 bottom. Almost 40% of drugs in clinical trials originated in China, and China took about 59% of global licensing deal value in the first ten months of 2026. Wood encourages exploring AI in healthcare.
Asia Pacific ex-Japan allocation changes: India up 2ppts to 14% (Overweight), Korea down 1ppt to 18% and Taiwan down 1ppt to 24% (both Underweight).

market_movers.rationale: 5Y CDS surged from 452bp to 1,163bp on 22 October. The DDTL 5.0 loan yield rose to 8.36%. Long-term contracts are priced at about a third of short-term rates.
5Y CDS rose from 153bp in early June to 329bp on 20 October. Its RPO is part of the US$2.5tn circular financing backlog.
Search growth slowed to 12% YoY and fell below half of revenue. Free cash flow was negative US$9bn in 3Q26 while capex guidance of US$195-205bn was held.
Online stores grew only 2% YoY. Free cash flow was negative US$35bn in 3Q26 while 2026 capex guidance of US$220bn was held.
Offered buyouts to about 60,000 staff and lowered 2026 capex guidance to US$170bn. Free cash flow remained positive at US$18.6bn.

sector_views.rationale: Semis were sold on the view that earnings momentum peaked and the second derivative turned. Memory stocks are down 40% from their June peak.
The US biotech ETF is up 139% from its April 2025 low. Chinese drug licensing is a driver, and AI drug design is called the most worthwhile AI application.
Any rally on an AI capex bust is an opportunity to sell, because fiscal dominance removes the flight-to-quality bid.

earnings_insights: Alphabet 3Q26, reported: search revenue +12% YoY to US$63bn (vs +19% in 1Q26 and +17% in 2Q26). Google Cloud revenue +103% YoY to US$30.7bn. Search was 49.7% of total revenue, down from 52.8% in 2Q26. Cloud was 24.1%, up from 20.7%.
Amazon 3Q26, reported: online stores revenue +2% YoY to US$68.5bn (vs +15% in 2Q26). AWS revenue +39% YoY to US$46bn. Online stores were 33.9% of revenue, down from 37.4% in 3Q25.
Free cash flow in 3Q26, reported: Amazon negative US$35bn, Alphabet negative US$9bn, Microsoft positive US$18.6bn.

Combined 3Q26 capex of the four hyperscalers was US$202bn, up 108% YoY. 2026 guidance: Microsoft US$170bn (cut from US$175bn), Amazon US$220bn, Alphabet US$195-205bn, Meta US$135-145bn (raised from US$130-145bn).
Consensus estimate: global AI stocks' earnings growth of about 100% in 2026, 30% in 2027 and 22% in 2028 (Jefferies quant).

macro_indicators.interpretation: AI-related investment contributed 1.39ppts, or 67%, of this growth.
The deficit normally rises about 6 points of GDP in a recession, so little room remains and Treasuries lose their safe-haven role in a downturn.
The rally reflects risk-off in AI stocks and hopes for restraint on spending. Wood sees it as a chance to sell bonds.
The drop reflects hopes that Trump abandons the Iran project after the mid-term defeat.
Gold traded near the bottom of the range over the past week.
Wood thinks credit stress means actual capex will fall short of this.

trade_ideas.description: Sell US Treasuries into any flight-to-quality rally triggered by an AI capex bust
trade_ideas.rationale: Fiscal dominance and a 6.2% of GDP deficit mean the Treasury market behaves like an emerging market in a recession.

trade_ideas.description: Diversify beyond AI equities (Jefferies quant strategy view)
trade_ideas.rationale: AI consensus earnings growth is expected to slow from about 100% in 2026 to 30% in 2027.

trade_ideas.description: Asia Pacific ex-Japan allocation: raise India to 14% (Overweight), cut Korea to 18% and Taiwan to 24% (Underweight)
trade_ideas.rationale: Taiwan and Korea carry the AI semiconductor supply chain, which is under pressure from the capex slowdown risk.
It is a developing thesis, unlike the supply-chain bottleneck trade.

risk_factors: Credit markets cut off funding to AI investment, ending the capex arms race.
Circular financing and US$2.5tn of RPOs across Microsoft, Amazon, Alphabet and Oracle.
Off-balance-sheet data center financing with private credit.
Repeal of OBBBA bonus depreciation and Democratic regulation of data centers and AI models.
Neocloud consolidation as credit is withdrawn.
AI cannibalising the search and e-commerce businesses.
Sudden reversal of Fed policy expectations from tightening to easing.
Fiscal dominance and Treasury market stress in a recession.

tension_points.bull_case: Capex still rose in 3Q26 (combined US$202bn, +108% YoY), TSMC is reportedly on course for US$75-80bn next year, rental demand for one-year contracts is strong, and there is no sign yet in real-world data of a peak.
tension_points.bear_case: Credit spreads and CDS have widened, long-term GPU rental contracts are priced at a third of short-term rates, free cash flow is negative at Amazon and Alphabet, AI earnings growth is expected to slow sharply, and memory stocks are already down 40%.
tension_points.what_invalidates: Tightening AI-related credit spreads, for example Oracle and CoreWeave CDS retracing from their October highs of 329bp and 1,163bp, would undercut the peak case. Spreads are the indicator the report says to monitor.

tension_points.bull_case: Investors initially buy the long end in a downturn, as shown by the 49bp fall in the 10-year yield from its peak.
tension_points.bear_case: Fiscal dominance and a 6.2% of GDP deficit mean the Treasury market behaves like an emerging market in a recession, so the rally is a chance to sell bonds.
